recommendations.rationale: A contact Raman probe measures liquid and solid samples and is comparatively tolerant of water, so one probe can look at mother liquor and crystals at the same spot; its bands are sharper than NIR bands, which matters for form-related information. Its signal is weak and can be swamped by fluorescence, so that must be checked on the real stream, with the laser excitation wavelength reported separately from the Raman shift.
recommendations.conditions: Applies as long as the stream's fluorescence background does not swamp the weak Raman bands.

solution_options.fusion_note: Fusion level: start with one model per method, then join the two blocks (block-scaled spectra or extracted scores) so that the block with more variables does not dominate. Both probes must look at the same small spot and the two data streams must be brought to a common time step, with a separate calibration and diagnostic kept for each instrument. Keep the fused model only if it beats the best single method on independent runs.

assessment.chemometrics_note: Plan one calibration per method first, then a fused model: both NIR and Raman calibrations are specific to the sample matrix and have to be re-validated after a change of matrix or composition (REF §5). NIR bands overlap broadly and need chemometric treatment (S01 p.10); the published in-line NIR + Raman example used low-level data fusion into one augmented matrix with PLS regression (S01 p.15). Reference data volume and validation on independent batches matter more than model complexity.
assessment.realtime_tracking_note: Both methods would run continuously in-line, so the two data streams must be aligned to a common time step and the dead time between the measurement ports accounted for before any result is used for control (S01 p.8).
assessment.future_direction: If the fused laboratory model shows a real gain, the later step is a compact multisensor system dedicated to this application rather than a full laboratory spectrometer set (S01 p.9).

proposal.what_would_change_it: Answers to the questions on solute and concentration range, on what 'crystal form' must distinguish, and on solvent, solids loading and turbidity decide whether Raman, NIR or the fusion is the better fit; if a single method fails the customer's accuracy criteria in the feasibility test, the fused option (O3) becomes the candidate. A clear, particle-free measurement point would also bring NIR transmission back into consideration.
proposal.next_step: Run the single-method feasibility test on representative crystalliser samples with independent reference values for both outputs, and build one model per method before any fused model.

assessment.brief_answer: Test one method at a time. On representative crystalliser samples, run a Raman probe first, with an NIR probe at the same point as the comparison, and independent reference values for solute concentration and crystal form. Fusion is a later hypothesis: worth testing only if a fused model beats the best single method on held-out runs. The deciding facts - solute, range, solvent, accuracy - are still open, so no final configuration can be fixed yet.
